I don't have a tiny house but I have some advice to new home owner.
DON'T trust your realtor, they are there for a paycheck.
Look at many houses.
Buy UNDER what you can afford. Insurance and taxes go up every year and your monthly payment will go up.
Get two home inspections for different people and not the one your realtor recommends.
If you can hear the outside world when it's empty, you can hear it when the house is full.
DON'T LOOK at the cosmetics.
This one is important. If the house is a fixer upper, it's going to have problems and you must likely will have to live in that for a long long time.

comments.text:
I think a large part of the problem is that tiny homes originally seemed like projects for handypeople who owned their own land or lot. They paid for materials as they were used and saved a ton of money by doing the work themselves.  This was a very affordable option for these people, who ended up owning a home outright for about 40k.  As always happens, people jumped on the bandwagon and went the tiny-home route as a solution  for the insane prices of even "moderately" priced starter homes.  They had no building experience and relied on the same developers and builders who were producing poorly built structures at inflated prices.
My boyfriend went the former route and now owns a cozy "mini" home on 5 acres for about 60k, including the land.  An electrician, he did all the wiring and much of the other finish work.  The dwelling allows for a bit of personal space, even when my boyfriend's teenaged son visits.  But it's due to the excellent design and thoughtful placement of EVERY feature of the home.  
This type of home can be a wonderful, cost-effective option, but it requires extensive planning and a lot of homework.  And in most cases a willingness to roll up one's sleeves and build some sweat equity!
